faqs.a: Five fields: minute (0-59), hour (0-23), day of month (1-31), month (1-12), day of week (0-6, where both 0 and 7 mean Sunday). * means every value, */n means every nth value, 1-5 is a range, and 1,15 is a list.
faqs.q: What do the five cron fields mean?

faqs.a: Use a step: */5 in the minute field means every 5 minutes. */2 in the hour field means every 2 hours. Steps also work on ranges, e.g. 9-17/2 means every 2 hours between 9:00 and 17:00.
faqs.q: How do I run something every 5 minutes?

faqs.a: Put 0 in minute and 9 in hour with everything else *: 0 9 * * *. For weekdays only, set day of week to 1-5: 0 9 * * 1-5. Note this uses the server's local timezone unless your scheduler says otherwise.
faqs.q: How do I schedule a daily 9 AM job?

faqs.a: When both are restricted, cron treats them as OR: the job runs when either matches. 0 0 1 * 0 runs at midnight on the 1st of the month AND every Sunday. To run only on the 1st, leave day of week as *.
faqs.q: What happens if I set both day of month and day of week?

faqs.a: Standard cron has no seconds field; the smallest unit is one minute. Some systems (Quartz, some Node schedulers) use six or seven fields with seconds first. This builder uses classic 5-field cron, which crontab, Kubernetes CronJobs and most Linux schedulers expect.
faqs.q: Why is there no seconds field?

faqs.a: Usually a timezone mismatch (cron runs in the server's timezone, often UTC), a crontab syntax the system rejects silently, or the cron daemon not running. Check the next-run preview in this builder against your server's date output to spot timezone gaps.
faqs.q: My cron job never runs. What should I check?

cron-builder.formula:
* * * * *
| | | | |
| | | | +-- day of week (0-6, 0 and 7 = Sunday)
| | | +---- month (1-12)
| | +------ day of month (1-31)
| +-------- hour (0-23)
+---------- minute (0-59)

* = every value, */n = every nth value, a-b = range, a,b = list.
When day of month AND day of week are both restricted, the job runs when EITHER matches.
howTo: Pick a preset for a common schedule, or tweak any field to build a custom expression.

Watch the expression, the plain-English description and the next 5 run times update live.
If a field shows an error, fix the value: each field has strict min/max limits.
Copy the verified expression into your crontab or scheduler configuration.
keyFacts: Cron schedules are five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week.
* means every possible value; */15 means every 15 units; 9-17 is a range; 1,15 is a list.
Both 0 and 7 mean Sunday in the day-of-week field.
Day of month and day of week combine with OR when both are restricted, not AND.
Cron has minute precision: there is no seconds field in classic 5-field cron.
Jobs run in the scheduler's timezone, which is often UTC on servers, not your local time.

cron-builder.quickAnswer: Pick a preset or customize each of the five fields (minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week) and this builder produces a valid cron expression with a plain-English description and the next 5 run times. For example, minute 0, hour 9, day of week Monday gives 0 9 * * 1, which means every Monday at 09:00. Field-level validation catches out-of-range values instantly.

cron-builder.workedExample:
Goal: run a backup every Monday at 09:00.
1. Preset: pick Weekly Monday, or set fields manually.
2. Minute: specific value 0. Hour: specific value 9.
3. Day of month: every (*). Month: every (*). Day of week: specific value 1 (Monday).
4. Expression: 0 9 * * 1.
5. Description: Every Monday at 09:00.
6. Next runs preview lists the coming Mondays at 09:00 in your local time.
Every 5 minutes would be: minute */5, everything else * -> */5 * * * *.
